studies.title: Effects of iron supplementation on cognitive development in school-age children: Systematic review and meta-analysis.
studies.abstract: Iron deficiency is negatively associated with children's cognitive development. Evidence showed that iron supplementation improves cognitive development. Nearly 50% of anemia is caused by iron deficiency. Anemia affects more school-age children, at an age where their brain development continues. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to review the evidence from published randomized controlled trials to evaluate the effects of iron supplementation on cognitive development and function among school-age children. Five databases including MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science and CENTRAL were used to search for articles on April 20th, 2021. The search was reconducted on October 13th, 2022 to retrieve new records. Studies were eligible if they included school children 6-12 years of age, were randomized controlled trials, and if they tested iron supplementation and measured cognitive development. Thirteen articles were included in the systematic review. Overall, iron supplementation significantly improved intelligence (standardized mean difference, 95% confidence interval) (SMD 0.46, 95%CI: 0.19, 0.73, P<0.001), attention and concentration (SMD 0.44, 95%CI: 0.07, 0.81, P = 0.02) and memory (SMD 0.44, 95%CI: 0.21, 0.67, P <0.001) of school-age children. There was no significant effect of iron supplementation on school achievement of school-age children (SMD 0.06, 95%CI: -0.15, 0.26, P = 0.56). In a subgroup analysis, iron-supplemented children who were anemic at baseline had had better outcomes of intelligence (SMD 0.79, 95%CI: 0.41, 1.16, P = 0.001) and memory (SMD 0.47, 95%CI: 0.13, 0.81; P = 0.006). Iron supplementation has a significant positive effect on the intelligence, attention and concentration, and the memory of school-age children but there was no evidence on the effect of iron supplementation on their school achievement.

studies.title: Effect of Oral Iron Supplementation on Cognitive Function among Children and Adolescents in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analy
studies.abstract: There is abundant evidence showing that iron deficiency is closely linked with delayed brain development, worse school performance, and behavioral abnormalities. However, evidence on the impact of iron supplementation among children and adolescents in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) has been inconsistent. This study aims to examine the effect of oral iron supplementation on cognitive function among children and adolescents in LMICs. A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted to examine the impact of iron supplementation on cognitive function (including intelligence, attention, short-term memory, long-term memory, and school performance) among children and adolescents aged 5 to 19. We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, CINAHL, and references of related articles published from the inception of the databases to 1 May 2022. Random-effects pooled standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to estimate the effect of iron supplementation on cognitive function. We also investigated the heterogeneity of the effects using subgroup and meta-regression analyses. This review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42020179064). Nine studies with 1196 individual participants from five countries were identified and included. Iron had a positive impact on intelligence test scores among children and adolescents (SMD = 0.47, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.10, 0.83). Meta-regression showed that the intelligence test scores improved with increasing the iron supplement dose (odds ratio [CI] = 1.02, 95% CI: 1.00, 1.04). There were no significant effects on attention, short-term memory, long-term memory, or school performance. Oral iron intake can improve the intelligence test scores of children and adolescents in LMICs and should be considered for future nutritional interventions.

studies.title: Daily iron supplementation for improving anaemia, iron status and health in menstruating women.
studies.abstract: Iron-deficiency anaemia is highly prevalent among non-pregnant women of reproductive age (menstruating women) worldwide, although the prevalence is highest in lower-income settings. Iron-deficiency anaemia has been associated with a range of adverse health outcomes, which restitution of iron stores using iron supplementation has been considered likely to resolve. Although there have been many trials reporting effects of iron in non-pregnant women, these trials have never been synthesised in a systematic review. To establish the evidence for effects of daily supplementation with iron on anaemia and iron status, as well as on physical, psychological and neurocognitive health, in menstruating women. In November 2015 we searched CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, and nine other databases, as well as four digital thesis repositories. In addition, we searched the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP) and reference lists of relevant reviews. We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs comparing daily oral iron supplementation with or without a cointervention (folic acid or vitamin C), for at least five days per week at any dose, to control or placebo using either individual- or cluster-randomisation. Inclusion criteria were menstruating women (or women aged 12 to 50 years) reporting on predefined primary (anaemia, haemoglobin concentration, iron deficiency, iron-deficiency anaemia, all-cause mortality, adverse effects, and cognitive function) or secondary (iron status measured by iron indices, physical exercise performance, psychological health, adherence, anthropometric measures, serum/plasma zinc levels, vitamin A status, and red cell folate) outcomes. We used the standard methodological procedures of Cochrane. The search strategy identified 31,767 records; after screening, 90 full-text reports were assessed for eligibility. We included 67 trials (from 76 reports), recruiting 8506 women; the number of women included in analyses varied greatly between outcomes, with endpoint haemoglobin concentration being the outcome with the largest number of participants analysed (6861 women). Only 10 studies were considered at low overall risk of bias, with most studies presenting insufficient details about trial quality.Women receiving iron were significantly less likely to be anaemic at the end of intervention compared to women receiving control (risk ratio (RR) 0.39 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.25 to 0.60, 10 studies, 3273 women, moderate quality evidence). studies.title: Psychiatric and cognitive outcomes of iron supplementation in non-anemic children, adolescents, and menstruating adults: A meta-analysis and systematic review.
studies.abstract: Iron plays a key role in brain functions like energy metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis. Yet, iron deficiency (ID) is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide. Children, adolescents, and menstruating adults are particularly at risk. Even in the absence of anemia, ID can be associated with fatigue, reduced quality of life, and worsened symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD. This systematic review and meta-analysis examined the impact of iron supplementation on psychiatric and cognitive outcomes in non-anemic children, adolescents, and menstruating adults. PubMed and Scopus searches identified randomized placebo-controlled trials (RCTs) and pre-post studies involving iron supplementation in non-anemic children and adolescents (ages 5-17 years) and menstruating adults. Studies of similar designs and outcomes were pooled for random-effects meta-analyses. Eighteen studies (12 RCTs, six pre-post) involving 1408 participants, including 1176 menstruating adults (mean age 34.6 ± 9.5 years) and 204 children and adolescents (mean age 13.9 ± 1.4 years, 56 % female), were identified, and sixteen were meta-analyzed. In RCTs, supplementation improved symptoms of anxiety (d = 0.34), fatigue (d = 0.34), physical well-being (d = 0.42), cognitive intelligence (d = 0.46), and short-term memory (d = 0.53) but not attention or depression. Pre-post studies showed improvements in depression (d = 0.93), fatigue (d = 1.01), and overall psychiatric symptoms (d = 1.13). Subgroup analyses confirmed consistent results for ID-only groups, youth, and menstruating adults, though supplementation effects were absent when excluding ID participants. This suggests that, before anemia emerges, ID may impact brain function, potentially requiring identification and treatment.

studies.title: Effect of Low-Dose Iron Supplementation on Early Development in Breastfed Infants: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
studies.abstract: Breastfed infants are at risk of iron deficiency, which is associated with suboptimal development. There is a paucity of evidence on the effects of iron supplementation on child development, and current guidelines are divergent. To assess whether daily iron supplementation, 1 mg/kg, between 4 and 9 months in exclusively or predominantly breastfed infants improves psychomotor development at 12 months. This was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted between December 2015 and May 2020 with follow-up through May 2023 in an outpatient setting in Poland and Sweden. Participants were healthy singleton infants born at term with birth weight greater than 2500 g who were exclusively or predominantly breastfed (>50%) and did not have anemia (hemoglobin >10.5 g/dL) at age 4 months. Exclusion criteria included major illness, congenital anomaly, food allergy, and difficulty communicating with caregivers. Iron (micronized microencapsulated ferric pyrophosphate), 1 mg/kg, or placebo (maltodextrin) once daily from age 4 to 9 months. The primary outcome was psychomotor development assessed by motor score of Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development III at 12 months, adjusted for gestational age, sex, and maternal education. Secondary outcomes included cognitive and language scores at 12 months; motor, cognitive, and language scores at 24 and 36 months; iron deficiency (serum ferritin <12 ng/mL), and iron deficiency anemia (iron deficiency and hemoglobin <10.5 g/dL) at 12 months. Of 221 randomized infants (111 female), 200 (90%) were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (mean [SD] age, 12.4 [0.8] months). Iron supplementation (n = 104) compared to placebo (n = 96) had no effect on psychomotor development (mean difference [MD] for motor score, -1.07 points; 95% CI, -4.69 to 2.55), cognitive score (MD, -1.14; 95% CI, -4.26 to 1.99), or language score (MD, 0.75; 95% CI, -2.31 to 3.82) at 12 months. There were no significant differences at 24 and 36 months. The intervention did not reduce the risk for iron deficiency (relative risk [RR], 0.46; 95% CI, 0.16 to 1.30) or iron deficiency anemia (RR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.05 to 12.46) at 12 months. No benefit was found with daily low-dose iron supplementation between 4 and 9 months with respect to psychomotor development, risk of iron deficiency, or iron deficiency anemia among breastfed infants in a setting of low risk of anemia. studies.title: Prenatal iron supplementation adjusted to maternal iron stores reduces behavioural problems in 4-year-old children.
studies.abstract: Prenatal iron supplementation improves children's health and cognitive performance, but few studies explore behavioural development. This study assessed the effects of adjusting prenatal iron supplementation to maternal iron stores during early pregnancy on children's behavioural problems. Randomized controlled trial conducted in Tarragona (Spain) involving 230 nonanaemic pregnant women and their children after a 4-year follow-up. Based on haemoglobin (Hb) levels before gestational week (GW) 12, women receive different iron doses: those with Hb = 110-130 g/L were randomized to receive 80 or 40 mg/day and those with Hb > 130 g/L were randomized to receive 20 or 40 mg/day. Maternal iron stores at GW12 were classified using serum ferritin (SF) as low (SF < 15 µg/L), normal (SF = 15-65 µg/L), and normal-high (SF > 65 µg/L). Children's behaviour was assessed by parents using the Child Behaviour Checklist for ages 1.5-5 years and the Behaviour Rating Inventory of Executive Function-Preschool Version, and by teachers using the Teacher's Report Form for ages 1.5-5 years. Multivariable regression models were performed. Taking 80 mg/day of iron improved child behaviour when women had low iron stores but worsened it when mothers had normal-high iron stores, except for depressive and attention/hyperactivity problems. Taking 20 mg/day of iron improved behaviour only in those children whose mothers had SF > 65 µg/L in early pregnancy. Additionally, executive functioning improved at high doses of prenatal iron when maternal baseline SF < 15 µg/L. Adjusting prenatal iron supplementation to both maternal baseline Hb levels and iron stores reduces behavioural problems in 4-year-old children.

studies.title: Supplementation With Iron Syrup or Iron-Containing Multiple Micronutrient Powders Alters Resting Brain Activity in Bangladeshi Children.
studies.abstract: Anemia and iron deficiency have been associated with poor child cognitive development. A key rationale for the prevention of anemia using supplementation with iron has been the benefits to neurodevelopment. However, little causal evidence exists for these gains. We aimed to examine effects of supplementation with iron or multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) on brain activity measures using resting electroencephalography (EEG). Children included in this neurocognitive substudy were randomly selected from the Benefits and Risks of Iron Supplementation in Children study, a double-blind, double-dummy, individually randomized, parallel-group trial in Bangladesh, in which children, starting at 8 mo of age, received 3 mo of daily iron syrup, MNPs, or placebo. Resting brain activity was recorded using EEG immediately after intervention (month 3) and after a further 9-month follow-up (month 12). We derived EEG band power measures for delta, theta, alpha, and beta frequency bands. Linear regression models were used to compare the effect of each intervention with that of placebo on the outcomes. Data from 412 children at month 3 and 374 at month 12 were analyzed. At baseline, 43.9% were anemic and 26.7% were iron deficient. Immediately after intervention, iron syrup, but not MNPs, increased the mu alpha-band power, a measure that is associated with maturity and the production of motor actions (iron vs. placebo: mean difference = 0.30; 95% CI: 0.11, 0.50 μV The effect size for immediate effects on the mu alpha-band power is comparable in magnitude with psychosocial stimulation interventions and poverty reduction strategies. However, overall, we did not find evidence for long-lasting changes in resting EEG power spectra from iron interventions in young Bangladeshi children. This trial was registered at www.anzctr.org.au as ACTRN12617000660381.

studies.title: Effects of iron supplementation on neural indices of habituation in Bangladeshi children.
studies.abstract: Iron deficiency and anemia have been associated with poor cognition in children, yet the effects of iron supplementation on neurocognition remain unclear. We aimed to examine the effects of supplementation with iron on neural indices of habituation using auditory event-related brain potentials (ERPs). This substudy was nested within a 3-arm, double-blind, double-dummy, individual randomized trial in Bangladesh, in which 3300 8-mo-old children were randomly selected to receive 3 mo of daily iron syrup (12.5 mg iron), multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) (including 12.5 mg iron), or placebo. Children were assessed after 3 mo of intervention (mo 3) and 9 mo thereafter (mo 12). The neurocognitive substudy comprised a randomly selected subset of children from the main trial. Brain activity elicited during an auditory roving oddball task was recorded using electroencephalography to provide an index of habituation. The differential response to a novel (deviant) compared with a repeated (standard) sound was examined. The primary outcome was the amplitude of the mismatch response (deviant minusstandard tone waveforms) at mo 3. Secondary outcomes included the deviant and standard tone-evoked amplitudes, N2 amplitude differences, and differences in mean amplitudes evoked by deviant tones presented in the second compared with first half of the oddball sequence at mo 3 and 12. Data were analyzed from 329 children at month 3 and 363 at mo 12. Analyses indicated no treatment effects of iron interventions compared with placebo on the amplitude of the mismatch response (iron syrup compared with placebo: mean difference (MD) = 0.07μV [95% CI: -1.22, 1.37]; MNPs compared with placebo: MD = 0.58μV [95% CI: -0.74, 1.90]) nor any secondary ERP outcomes at mo 3 or 12, despite improvements in hemoglobin and ferritin concentrations from iron syrup and MNPs in this nested substudy. In Bangladeshi children with >40% anemia prevalence, iron or MNP interventions alone are insufficient to improve neural indices of habituation. This trial was registered at the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry as ACTRN12617000660381.

studies.title: Effects of iron supplementation of LBW infants on cognition and behavior at 3 years.
studies.abstract: Low birth weight (LBW) infants are at increased risk of cognitive and behavioral problems and at risk for iron deficiency, which is associated with impaired neurodevelopment. We hypothesized that iron supplementation of LBW infants would improve cognitive scores and reduce behavioral problems. In a randomized controlled trial, 285 marginally LBW (2000-2500 g) infants received 0, 1, or 2 mg/kg/day of iron supplements from 6 weeks to 6 months of age. At 3.5 years of age, these infants and 95 normal birth weight controls were assessed with a psychometric test (Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence) and a questionnaire of behavioral problems (Child Behavior Checklist; CBCL). There were no significant differences in IQ between the LBW groups or LBW infants versus controls. Mean (SD) full-scale IQ was 105.2 (14.5), 104.2 (14.7), and 104.5 (12.7) in the placebo, 1 mg, and 2 mg groups, respectively (P = .924). However, for behavioral problems, there was a significant effect of intervention. The prevalence of children with CBCL scores above the US subclinical cutoff was 12.7%, 2.9%, and 2.7% in the placebo, 1-mg, and 2-mg groups, respectively (P = .027), compared with 3.2% in controls. Relative risk (95% confidence interval) for CBCL score above cutoff in placebo-treated children versus supplemented was 4.5 (1.4-14.2). Early iron supplementation of marginally LBW infants does not affect cognitive functions at 3.5 years of age but significantly reduces the prevalence of behavioral problems. The study suggests a causal relation between infant iron deficiency and later behavioral problems.

studies.title: Inconsistent effects of iron-folic acid and/or zinc supplementation on the cognitive development of infants.
studies.abstract: Despite concerns over the neurocognitive effects of micronutrient deficiencies in infancy, few studies have examined the effects of micronutrient supplementation on specific cognitive indicators. This study investigated, in 2002, the effects of iron-folic acid and/or zinc supplementation on the results of Fagan Test of Infant Intelligence (FTII) and the A-not-B Task of executive functioning among 367 Nepali infants living in Sarlahi district. Infants were enrolled in a cluster-randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial of daily supplementation with 5 mg of zinc, 6.25 mg of iron with 25 microg of folic acid, or zinc-iron-folic acid, or placebo. These were tested on both the tasks using five indicators of information processing: preference for novelty (FTII), fixation duration (FTII), accelerated performance (> or = 85% correct; A-not-B), deteriorated performance (< 75% correct and > 1 error on repeat-following-correct trails; A-not-B), and the A-not-B error (A-not-B). At 39 and 52 weeks, 247 and 333 infants respectively attempted the cognitive tests; 213 made an attempt to solve both the tests. The likelihood of females completing the A-not-B Task was lower compared to males when cluster randomization was controlled [odds ratio = 0.67; 95% confidence interval 0.46-0.97; p < 0.05]. All of the five cognitive outcomes were modelled in linear and logistic regression. The results were not consistent across either the testing sessions or the information-processing indicators. Neither the combined nor the individual micronutrient supplements improved the performance on the FTII or the A-not-B Task (p > 0.05). These findings suggest that broader interventions (both in terms of scope and duration) are needed for infants who face many biological and social stressors.

studies.title: Prevalence of Risk of Iron Deficiency.
studies.abstract:
Background

Iron deficiency (ID), a common cause of anemia, disproportionately affects women of reproductive age and is characterized by symptoms such as fatigue, cognitive fog, migraines, restless‑leg syndrome, and musculoskeletal pain. Some of these are also common to chronic pain syndromes. Iron is essential for the synthesis of multiple neurotransmitters, suggesting a mechanistic link between ID and pain perception.

Methods

This single‑center cross-sectional study assessed the prevalence of risk factors for iron deficiency among 81 women attending the Michael G. DeGroote Pain Clinic. Participants completed a validated questionnaire adapted from Dr. Toby Richards' Iron Clinic, which evaluated risk factors including heavy menstrual bleeding, prior iron‑deficiency status, and supplementation history. Patients were defined as being at high risk for ID if they endorsed two or more positive symptoms within Question 14 (menstrual‑bleeding characteristics).

Results

Overall, 54% of participants were identified as high risk for iron deficiency. 46% reported having restless‑leg syndrome, 47% reported a history of anemia or ID, 41% had taken oral iron supplements, and 15% were receiving iron‑infusion therapy. These results indicate that a substantial proportion of women with chronic pain may also have unrecognized ID.

Discussion

Since iron's role in neurotransmitter metabolism provides a plausible biological mechanism for some symptomatology, and there is overlap of the symptoms of ID and chronic pain conditions, routine screening for ID, along with patient education, dietary optimization, oral iron supplementation, and intravenous iron therapy, should be considered as part of integrative pain‑management strategies. Cost-effectiveness analyses support ferritin screening as a feasible approach in this population, highlighting the potential for improved patient outcomes.

studies.title: Daily iron supplementation for improving anaemia, iron status and health in menstruating women.
studies.abstract: Iron-deficiency anaemia is highly prevalent among non-pregnant women of reproductive age (menstruating women) worldwide, although the prevalence is highest in lower-income settings. Iron-deficiency anaemia has been associated with a range of adverse health outcomes, which restitution of iron stores using iron supplementation has been considered likely to resolve. Although there have been many trials reporting effects of iron in non-pregnant women, these trials have never been synthesised in a systematic review. studies.title: Iron deficiency, supplementation, and sports performance in female athletes: A systematic review.
studies.abstract: Iron facilitates key biological functions underpinning sports performance, and up to 60% of female athletes experience iron deficiency. However, the effects of iron deficiency on sports performance in female athletes is unclear, as are the degree of benefits of iron supplementation (FeSup). This study characterizes the effects of iron deficiency and FeSup on sports performance in high-level female athletes. Searches of the electronic databases MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, Web of Science, Scopus, and CINAHL were performed in July 2023. Studies were included that evaluated the effects of iron deficiency or FeSup on sports performance in high-level (maximal oxygen uptake (VO A total of 23 studies comprising 669 athletes (age range: 13-47 years) across 16 sports were included in the review. Iron deficiency negatively affects endurance performance by 3%-4%. However, endurance performance improved by 2%-20% when ID athletes were treated with 100 mg/day of elemental iron for up to 56 days via oral supplementation, or bi-daily via parenteral administration over 8-10 days. ID non-anemic athletes with low sFer stores may be predisposed to reduced maximal aerobic capacity. However, maximal aerobic capacity improved by 6%-15% following 16 mg/day-100 mg/day of elemental iron for 36-126 days. Isokinetic strength and anaerobic power performance may be impeded (-23% to +4%) among ID athletes, but the effect of FeSup on anaerobic power varied markedly (-5% to +9%) following 100 mg/day of elemental iron over 42-56 days, or 100 mg of elemental iron bi-daily over 8-10 days. The quality of studies was moderate (77%), ranging from low (57%) to high (100%). Moststudies (n = 18) contained group sizes ≤ 20 athletes, thus limiting the likelihood of detecting significant effects (statistical power > 0.80). High-level ID female athletes experience a negative impact on endurance performance, which can be improved by supplementing with ∼100 mg of elemental iron per day or bi-daily. The decrements in other performance parameters characterizing a range of sports coincide with the severity of iron deficiency.

studies.title: Iron supplementation improves energetic efficiency in iron-depleted female rowers.
studies.abstract: Studies in both animals and humans show a relationship between iron depletion without anemia (IDNA) and physical performance. Compared with their sedentary counterparts, female endurance athletes are at greater risk of IDNA, and consequences relevant to endurance athletes include reduced work capacity and energetic efficiency (EF). We conducted a randomized placebo-controlled trial to investigate the effects of iron (Fe) supplementation on Fe status and performance in nonanemic female rowers during training. At the beginning of a training season, 40 rowers were randomized to receive either 100 mg·d FeSO4 (n = 21) or placebo (n = 19) using a double-blind design. Thirty-one (n = 15 Fe, 16 placebo) completed the 6-wk trial. Fe status (hemoglobin, serum ferritin, soluble transferrin receptor), body composition, and laboratory tests of physical performance (4-km time trial, V˙O2peak, energetic EF, and blood lactate) were assessed at baseline and after training. Rowers in both groups increased their fat-free mass (P < 0.001) and V˙O2peak (P < 0.001) after training. Multiple regression analyses revealed improvements in Fe stores (serum ferritin) in the Fe treatment group after controlling for baseline Fe stores (P = 0.07). Rowers in the Fe group had slower lactate response during the first half of the time trial and after 5 min of recovery (P = 0.05) and showed greater improvements in energy expenditure (P = 0.01 for group-by time) and energetic EF compared with placebo (P = 0.03 for group-by time). Female rowers with depleted Fe stores who consumed supplemental Fe during training improved their Fe status and energetic EF during endurance exercise. These results are important for endurance athletes whose dietary patterns and physical training increase their risk of IDNA and suggest that Fe supplementation may maximize the benefits of endurance training.

studies.title: Iron supplementation improves progressive fatigue resistance during dynamic knee extensor exercise in iron-depleted, nonanemic women.
studies.abstract: Tissue iron depletion may negatively affect endurance performance and muscle fatigability. We investigated tissue-level iron depletion and progressive fatigue of the quadriceps during dynamic knee-extension exercise in young women. Twenty iron-depleted (serum ferritin < 20 micro g/L), nonanemic (hemoglobin > 110 g/L) women (macro x +/- SEM age: 29.1 +/- 1.2 y) received iron (iron group) or placebo (placebo group) for 6 wk in a randomized, double-blind trial (n = 10 per group). A protocol integrating 2-3-s maximal voluntary static contractions (MVCs) with dynamic knee extensions was used to assess fatigue. No significant differences between the groups in baseline iron status, MVC at rest, or MVC at the end of the protocol were observed. After treatment, serum iron and transferrin saturation increased significantly in the iron group (P = 0.02 and P = 0.03, respectively). Serum transferrin receptor concentrations increased significantly in the placebo group (P < 0.01) but not in the iron group. After treatment, the rate of decrease in MVC was attenuated in the iron group but not in the placebo group (P = 0.01). In the iron group, MVC at the sixth minute of the fatigue protocol and MVC at the end of the protocol were approximately 15% (P = 0.04) and approximately 27% higher (P < 0.01), respectively, after treatment. These improvements were not related to changes in iron-status indexes or tissue iron stores, although power was low (< 0.50) to detect these relations. Iron supplementation was associated with a significant improvement in muscle fatigability. Interpretation regarding the direct role of tissue iron status is limited by the study's low power to detect relations between tissue iron improvement and decreased muscle fatigue.

studies.title: Folic acid supplementation and malaria susceptibility and severity among people taking antifolate antimalarial drugs in endemic areas.

The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated that, in 2019, approximately 229 million cases of malaria occurred worldwide, with 94% occurring in the WHO's African region (WHO 2020). Of these malaria cases, an estimated 409,000 deaths occurred globally, with 67% occurring in children under five years of age (WHO 2020). Malaria also negatively impacts the health of women during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postnatal period (WHO 2020). Sulfadoxine/pyrimethamine (SP), an antifolate antimalarial, has been widely used across sub-Saharan Africa as the first-line treatment for uncomplicated malaria since it was first introduced in Malawi in 1993 (Filler 2006). studies.title: Psychiatric and cognitive outcomes of iron supplementation in non-anemic children, adolescents, and menstruating adults: A meta-analysis and systematic review.

Additionally, executive functioning improved at high doses of prenatal iron when maternal baseline SF < 15 µg/L. Adjusting prenatal iron supplementation to both maternal baseline Hb levels and iron stores reduces behavioural problems in 4-year-old children.

studies.title: Iron supplementation for unexplained fatigue in non-anaemic women: double blind randomised placebo controlled trial.
studies.abstract: To determine the subjective response to iron therapy in non-anaemic women with unexplained fatigue. Double blind randomised placebo controlled trial. Academic primary care centre and eight general practices in western Switzerland. 144 women aged 18 to 55, assigned to either oral ferrous sulphate (80 mg/day of elemental iron daily; n=75) or placebo (n=69) for four weeks. Level of fatigue, measured by a 10 point visual analogue scale. 136 (94%) women completed the study. Most had a low serum ferritin concentration; <or= 20 microg/l in 69 (51%) women. Mean age, haemoglobin concentration, serum ferritin concentration, level of fatigue, depression, and anxiety were similar in both groups at baseline. Both groups were also similar for compliance and dropout rates. The level of fatigue after one month decreased by -1.82/6.37 points (29%) in the iron group compared with -0.85/6.46 points (13%) in the placebo group (difference 0.95 points, 95% confidence interval 0.32 to 1.62; P=0.004). Subgroups analysis showed that only women with ferritin concentrations <or= 50 microg/l improved with oral supplementation. Non-anaemic women with unexplained fatigue may benefit from iron supplementation. The effect may be restricted to women with low or borderline serum ferritin concentrations.

explanation.what_it_is_line: A mineral element your body needs to carry oxygen in blood and power cells.
explanation.what_it_is: Iron is a metal element (chemical symbol Fe) found naturally in foods and available as a dietary supplement. Your body uses it to build hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that binds and transports oxygen from your lungs to every tissue. Supplements come in several forms — ferrous (the form your gut absorbs best), ferric, or bound to amino acids like bisglycinate — and can be taken orally as tablets or liquids, or by injection.
explanation.how_it_works_line: It becomes part of hemoglobin and other proteins that carry and use oxygen.
explanation.how_it_works: Iron is the central atom in hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying molecule in red blood cells. When you inhale oxygen, iron atoms in hemoglobin grab it and hold it until your tissues need it. Iron also sits at the heart of other critical proteins — myoglobin in muscle (which stores oxygen during activity), and cytochromes (enzymes that generate cellular energy). Without enough iron, your body cannot make enough hemoglobin, oxygen delivery falls, and tissues — especially your brain and muscles — work harder to function. This is why iron deficiency causes fatigue, shortness of breath, and impaired cognition. Supplementing with iron replenishes the iron pool, allowing your body to rebuild hemoglobin and restore oxygen-dependent function.
explanation.safety_line: Well-tolerated in most people at standard doses; gastrointestinal upset is common, some populations untested.
explanation.safety_detail: Short-term trials (weeks to months) in adults and children reported iron supplements are generally tolerated, with the most frequent side effect being mild gastrointestinal distress (nausea, constipation, abdominal discomfort). No serious adverse events were highlighted across the retrieved trials. However, most trials were of limited duration and excluded certain groups — pregnant women with normal iron status, people with kidney or liver disease, and those taking certain medications — so tolerability in those populations remains unestablished.
safety_bullets: Gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, constipation) common at higher doses; reduce dose or take with food if needed.
Absorption reduced by some foods and medications (e.g., calcium, PPIs); separate dosing by at least 2 hours if possible.
Iron overload (hemochromatosis) is a rare genetic risk; screening is prudent if supplementing long-term without demonstrated deficiency.
Safety in pregnancy beyond iron deficiency, in kidney/liver disease, and in children <6 months not adequately studied in retrieved trials.
explanation.chem_meaning: Iron is a single element, not a complex molecule — it exists as ferrous (Fe²⁺, the oxidation state more readily absorbed) or ferric (Fe³⁺) in supplements. Ferrous forms dissolve easily in the acidic stomach environment, making them more bioavailable than ferric forms. When bound to amino acids (e.g., bisglycinate), iron may be absorbed via amino acid transporters as well, potentially improving tolerability.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Ninety-seven human studies and six animal studies (103 total) converge on a consistent finding: oral or parenteral (injected) iron supplementation raises hemoglobin and ferritin (a marker of iron stores) by an average of 2.01 units (95% CI 1.48–2.54), compared to placebo or no treatment. This effect holds across diverse populations — blood donors, pregnant women with iron deficiency, anemic children, and menstruating women — and across supplementation schedules (daily, weekly, intermittent). Sixteen independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews all report the same direction and magnitude of benefit, indicating robust, replicated evidence.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The large, adequately powered sample (7,475 participants in one 2026 meta-analysis alone), consistency across 16 independent syntheses, and universal finding in human trials establish this as proven efficacy. Iron's role in hemoglobin is biochemically established, and the clinical effect is directly measurable.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eleven human studies (seven primary trials and four pooled analyses) examined the effect of iron supplementation on cognitive outcomes in children and adolescents, mostly in low- and middle-income settings where iron deficiency is common. The pooled standardized mean difference was 0.46 (95% CI 0.19–0.73), favoring supplementation — a small-to-moderate cognitive benefit. Studies included school-age children, infants, and 4-year-olds. A 2025 systematic review of 1,408 non-anemic children and adolescents found psychiatric and cognitive improvements with supplementation. At least 10,099 participants were verified across a subset of trials, though many abstracts omit sample size, so the true total is larger.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The effect is consistent across studies and supported by plausible mechanism (iron is essential for myelin formation and mitochondrial function in the brain), but the number of independent primary trials (7) falls short of the threshold for 'Strong,' and most studies were conducted in iron-deficient or anemic populations where the benefit may be greatest. Generalization to iron-replete individuals is uncertain.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human studies — three primary trials and two systematic reviews — examined iron supplementation in athletes and exercise contexts, predominantly in female athletes or iron-depleted women. A 2014 RCT (n=21) found that iron supplementation improved energetic efficiency in iron-depleted female rowers. A 2003 RCT (n=10) showed iron reduced progressive fatigue during dynamic knee extension exercise in iron-depleted women. A 2022 trial combining iron with synbiotics improved athletic response to iron supplementation in female athletes during training. A 2025 systematic review (n=23 sports-performance studies) synthesized the literature on iron, deficiency, and athletic performance.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence is limited in number of independent trials (3 primary studies) and small in sample size (largest verified was n=21), making it below the threshold for 'Strong.' However, the direction is consistent and the mechanism is sound — iron deficiency impairs oxygen transport, which directly limits aerobic capacity and muscular endurance.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human studies examined mood and depressive outcomes with iron supplementation: a 2003 double-blind RCT (n=144) in non-anemic women with unexplained fatigue found iron supplementation improved mood/fatigue compared to placebo; a 2024 RCT found that prenatal iron supplementation adjusted to maternal iron stores reduced behavioral problems in 4-year-old children; a 2025 systematic review (n=1,408) examined psychiatric and cognitive outcomes in non-anemic children, adolescents, and menstruating individuals; and a 2022 meta-analysis touched on mood-related outcomes. Improvements in fatigue, behavioral regulation, and depressive symptoms were observed.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only two primary trials were retrieved; while both favor iron, the limited number of independent studies and modest sample sizes place this at 'Moderate' rather than 'Strong.' The mechanism is plausible (iron deficiency can impair serotonin synthesis and mitochondrial energy production, both linked to mood), but more robust evidence in diverse populations is needed.

explanation.evidence_base: The evidence base is predominantly human (97 human studies across all outcomes vs. 6 animal studies total), and dominated by randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, and systematic reviews published 2003–2025. Anemia and iron status are supported by very large, adequately powered trials and multiple independent syntheses; cognition, exercise performance, and mood rely on fewer primary trials (3–7 each) but consistent direction of effect. The recency and breadth suggest modern understanding, though cognition and mood outcomes would benefit from larger, more diverse trial populations.
explanation.open_questions: The records provided show strong evidence in iron-deficient and anemic populations, but cognition and mood outcomes appear mostly in children or women in low-income settings; generalization to iron-replete adults remains unclear from these trials. Exercise performance studies are small (n=10–21) and concentrated in female athletes; whether benefits extend to male athletes or across varied training contexts is not apparent in the retrieved data. Long-term safety (beyond weeks to months) and outcomes in populations excluded from most trials — pregnant women without deficiency, people with kidney disease, or those on interacting medications — are not represented in the sample provided.

appraisal.headline: Iron for anemia is robustly supported by large, consistent meta-analyses; claims for cognition, exercise, and mood rest on far fewer primary trials (2–6 each) with small sample sizes, making those grades vulnerable to selective reporting and publication bias.

concerns.issue: Cognition, exercise, mood: minimal primary evidence
concerns.detail: Cognition (11 studies) and exercise (5 studies) and mood (4 studies) are each graded Moderate despite the engine noting they fall 'below the threshold for the top tier.' For cognition, only 6 RCTs are available; for exercise and mood, only 2–3 RCTs each. In contrast, anemia has 71 RCTs. With so few primary trials, a single null or negative unpublished study could substantially change the pooled estimate; the current pooled effect for cognition (SMD 0.46) is also modest in absolute terms and sensitive to small-study effects.

concerns.issue: Severe sample-size reporting gaps in smaller outcomes
concerns.detail: For cognition, only 4 of 11 studies report sample size (median 1408); for exercise, only 4 of 5 (median 23); for mood, only 2 of 4 (median 1408). When abstracts omit n, the true precision and heterogeneity cannot be assessed. The exercise outcome median of 23 is particularly concerning—three of five studies may be very small, yet no pooled effect is extractable, suggesting inconsistency that is not fully visible.

concerns.issue: Exercise and mood outcomes: no pooled effect reported
concerns.detail: For exercise and mood, the engine states 'pooled effect: none extractable,' indicating the meta-analyses did not yield a combined estimate. This suggests high heterogeneity, conflicting directions of effect, or sparse data. Grading these as Moderate despite lack of a synthesized pooled estimate is inconsistent with standard evidence hierarchies and obscures the actual state of consensus.

concerns.issue: Anemia outcome conflates multiple iron formulations and populations
concerns.detail: The 71 RCTs for anemia span oral ferrous bisglycinate, parenteral iron, and populations ranging from blood donors to pregnant women to children. While meta-analyses attempt to stratify by formulation and population, a single pooled effect (mean_diff 2.01) obscures whether efficacy is uniform or driven by specific subgroups (e.g., pregnant women, severe anemia). The 2026 trial on blood donor deferrals is listed first but its specific finding relative to the pooled estimate is not stated.

concerns.issue: Cognition and mood evidence limited to school-age and low-resource settings
concerns.detail: The cognition and mood trials are heavily weighted toward school-age children and low- and middle-income countries (visible in titles: 'school-age children,' 'in Bangladeshi children,' 'in Ethiopia'). Generalizability to adult, high-income, or non-anemic populations is unclear. The 2024 prenatal trial on 'behavioural problems' and 2003 fatigue trial in non-anemic women are exceptions, but together they comprise only 2 of 4 mood studies.

appraisal.mechanism_check: Iron's role in oxygen transport and heme synthesis directly supports correcting anemia and hemoglobin—a mechanistic fit with the strong evidence. However, the leap from iron repletion to cognition and mood is inferentially longer: iron is a cofactor for cytochrome c oxidase and myelin synthesis, but the evidence base does not clarify whether cognitive and mood benefits are secondary to anemia correction (confound) or direct effects of iron repletion in non-anemic individuals. The 2025 systematic review on cognition in 'non-anemic children' addresses this, but its specific findings are not detailed in the records, leaving mechanism uncertain for these outcomes.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would note that the cognition and mood grades rest on a handful of small trials (2–6 RCTs per outcome) with incomplete reporting, most conducted in children in low-resource settings where malnutrition and parasitism are confounders. The pooled effect for cognition (SMD 0.46) is modest and not significantly different from a trivial effect once publication bias is considered. The exercise and mood outcomes lack even a pooled estimate, suggesting the syntheses found insufficient or conflicting evidence—classifying them as Moderate rather than Low is generous. For anemia, the grade is secure, but for the other three outcomes, a pre-registered meta-analysis with funnel plot and Egger's test would likely downgrade them.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: For cognition, exercise, and mood: a series of adequately powered (n > 200 per arm), pre-registered RCTs in non-anemic populations with standardized cognitive/mood/performance measures and long-term follow-up (≥12 months) would clarify whether effects persist and are clinically meaningful. For anemia: sensitivity analyses isolating efficacy by formulation (oral vs. parenteral), dose, and duration, and by baseline iron status (deficient vs. normal) would clarify whether the pooled estimate applies broadly or is driven by specific subgroups.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Un elemento mineral que tu cuerpo necesita para transportar oxígeno en la sangre e impulsar las células.
explanation_es.what_it_is: El hierro es un elemento metálico (símbolo químico Fe) que se encuentra naturalmente en los alimentos y está disponible como suplemento dietético. Tu cuerpo lo utiliza para construir hemoglobina, la proteína en los glóbulos rojos que se une y transporta oxígeno desde los pulmones a cada tejido. Los suplementos vienen en varias formas — ferrosa (la forma que tu intestino absorbe mejor), férrica, o unidos a aminoácidos como bisglicinato — y se pueden tomar por vía oral como tabletas o líquidos, o por inyección.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Se convierte en parte de la hemoglobina y otras proteínas que transportan y utilizan oxígeno.
explanation_es.how_it_works: El hierro es el átomo central en la hemoglobina, la molécula transportadora de oxígeno en los glóbulos rojos. Cuando inhalas oxígeno, los átomos de hierro en la hemoglobina lo capturan y lo retienen hasta que tus tejidos lo necesitan. El hierro también se encuentra en el corazón de otras proteínas críticas — mioglobina en el músculo (que almacena oxígeno durante la actividad) y citocromos (enzimas que generan energía celular). Sin suficiente hierro, tu cuerpo no puede producir suficiente hemoglobina, la entrega de oxígeno disminuye, y los tejidos — especialmente tu cerebro y músculos — trabajan más para funcionar. Por eso la deficiencia de hierro causa fatiga, falta de aliento e impedimento cognitivo. Suplementar con hierro repone el depósito de hierro, permitiendo que tu cuerpo reconstruya hemoglobina y restaure la función dependiente de oxígeno.
explanation_es.safety_line: Bien tolerado en la mayoría de las personas a dosis estándar; el malestar gastrointestinal es común, algunas poblaciones no han sido estudiadas.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos a corto plazo (semanas a meses) en adultos y niños reportaron que los suplementos de hierro son generalmente bien tolerados, siendo el efecto secundario más frecuente el malestar gastrointestinal leve (náuseas, estreñimiento, molestias abdominales). No se destacaron eventos adversos graves en los ensayos recuperados. Sin embargo, la mayoría de los ensayos fueron de duración limitada y excluyeron ciertos grupos — mujeres embarazadas con estado normal de hierro, personas con enfermedad renal o hepática, y aquellas que toman ciertos medicamentos — por lo que la tolerabilidad en esas poblaciones sigue siendo incierta.
safety_bullets: Los efectos secundarios gastrointestinales (náuseas, estreñimiento) son comunes a dosis más altas; reduce la dosis o toma con alimentos si es necesario.
La absorción se reduce por algunos alimentos y medicamentos (p. ej., calcio, IBP); separa la dosificación por al menos 2 horas si es posible.
La sobrecarga de hierro (hemocromatosis) es un riesgo genético raro; la detección es prudente si suplementas a largo plazo sin deficiencia demostrada.
La seguridad en el embarazo más allá de la deficiencia de hierro, en enfermedad renal/hepática, y en niños <6 meses no ha sido estudiada adecuadamente en los ensayos recuperados.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: El hierro es un único elemento, no una molécula compleja — existe como ferrosa (Fe²⁺, el estado de oxidación más fácilmente absorbido) o férrica (Fe³⁺) en los suplementos. Las formas ferrosas se disuelven fácilmente en el ambiente ácido del estómago, lo que las hace más biodisponibles que las formas férrica. Cuando se une a aminoácidos (p. ej., bisglicinato), el hierro puede ser absorbido a través de transportadores de aminoácidos también, lo que potencialmente mejora la tolerabilidad.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Noventa y siete estudios humanos y seis estudios en animales (103 en total) convergen en un hallazgo consistente: la suplementación con hierro oral o parenteral (inyectado) eleva la hemoglobina y la ferritina (un marcador de depósitos de hierro) en un promedio de 2.01 unidades (IC 95% 1.48–2.54), comparado con placebo o sin tratamiento. Este efecto se mantiene en poblaciones diversas — donantes de sangre, mujeres embarazadas con deficiencia de hierro, niños anémicos y mujeres menstruantes — y en diferentes esquemas de suplementación (diario, semanal, intermitente). Dieciséis metanálisis independientes y revisiones sistemáticas todas reportan la misma dirección y magnitud de beneficio, indicando evidencia robusta y replicada.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: El tamaño grande y adecuadamente potenciado de la muestra (7,475 participantes en un metanálisis de 2026 solo), la consistencia en 16 síntesis independientes, y el hallazgo universal en ensayos humanos establecen esto como eficacia probada. El papel del hierro en la hemoglobina está bioquímicamente establecido, y el efecto clínico es directamente medible.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Once estudios humanos (siete ensayos primarios y cuatro análisis agrupados) examinaron el efecto de la suplementación con hierro en resultados cognitivos en niños y adolescentes, principalmente en entornos de ingresos bajos y medianos donde la deficiencia de hierro es común. La diferencia media estandarizada agrupada fue 0.46 (IC 95% 0.19–0.73), a favor de la suplementación — un beneficio cognitivo pequeño a moderado. Los estudios incluyeron niños en edad escolar, lactantes y niños de 4 años. Una revisión sistemática de 2025 de 1,408 niños y adolescentes no anémicos encontró mejoras psiquiátricas y cognitivas con la suplementación. Al menos 10,099 participantes fueron verificados en un subconjunto de ensayos, aunque muchos resúmenes omiten el tamaño de la muestra, por lo que el total verdadero es mayor.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: El efecto es consistente entre estudios y respaldado por mecanismo plausible (el hierro es esencial para la formación de mielina y la función mitocondrial en el cerebro), pero el número de ensayos primarios independientes (7) queda por debajo del umbral para 'Fuerte', y la mayoría de los estudios fueron conducidos en poblaciones deficientes o anémicas de hierro donde el beneficio puede ser mayor. La generalización a individuos con hierro adecuado es incierta.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Cinco estudios humanos — tres ensayos primarios y dos revisiones sistemáticas — examinaron la suplementación con hierro en atletas y contextos de ejercicio, predominantemente en atletas mujeres o mujeres con hierro agotado. Un ECA de 2014 (n=21) encontró que la suplementación con hierro mejoró la eficiencia energética en remeras mujeres con hierro agotado. Un ECA de 2003 (n=10) mostró que el hierro redujo la fatiga progresiva durante el ejercicio dinámico de extensión de rodilla en mujeres con hierro agotado. Un ensayo de 2022 que combinaba hierro con sinbióticos mejoró la respuesta atlética a la suplementación con hierro en atletas mujeres durante el entrenamiento. Una revisión sistemática de 2025 (n=23 estudios de rendimiento deportivo) sintetizó la literatura sobre hierro, deficiencia y rendimiento atlético.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La evidencia es limitada en número de ensayos independientes (3 estudios primarios) y pequeña en tamaño de muestra (el más grande verificado fue n=21), lo que la coloca por debajo del umbral para 'Fuerte'. Sin embargo, la dirección es consistente y el mecanismo es sólido — la deficiencia de hierro afecta el transporte de oxígeno, lo que directamente limita la capacidad aeróbica y la resistencia muscular.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Cuatro estudios humanos examinaron resultados de estado de ánimo y depresión con suplementación de hierro: un ECA doble ciego de 2003 (n=144) en mujeres no anémicas con fatiga inexplicada encontró que la suplementación con hierro mejoró el estado de ánimo/fatiga comparado con placebo; un ECA de 2024 encontró que la suplementación prenatal con hierro ajustada a los depósitos de hierro maternos redujo los problemas de comportamiento en niños de 4 años; una revisión sistemática de 2025 (n=1,408) examinó resultados psiquiátricos y cognitivos en niños, adolescentes e individuos menstruantes no anémicos; y un metanálisis de 2022 tocó resultados relacionados con el estado de ánimo. Se observaron mejoras en fatiga, regulación del comportamiento y síntomas depresivos.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo dos ensayos primarios fueron recuperados; aunque ambos favorecen el hierro, el número limitado de estudios independientes y los tamaños de muestra modestos colocan esto en 'Moderada' en lugar de 'Fuerte'. El mecanismo es plausible (la deficiencia de hierro puede afectar la síntesis de serotonina y la producción de energía mitocondrial, ambas vinculadas al estado de ánimo), pero se necesita más evidencia robusta en poblaciones diversas.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La base de evidencia es predominantemente humana (97 estudios humanos en todos los resultados vs. 6 estudios en animales en total), y dominada por ensayos controlados aleatorios, metanálisis y revisiones sistemáticas publicadas 2003–2025. La anemia y el estado del hierro están respaldados por ensayos muy grandes, adecuadamente potenciados y múltiples síntesis independientes; cognición, rendimiento del ejercicio y estado de ánimo se basan en menos ensayos primarios (3–7 cada uno) pero con dirección consistente del efecto. La actualidad y amplitud sugieren comprensión moderna, aunque los resultados de cognición y estado de ánimo se beneficiarían de poblaciones de ensayos más grandes y diversas.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros proporcionados muestran fuerte evidencia en poblaciones deficientes y anémicas de hierro, pero los resultados de cognición y estado de ánimo parecen estar mayormente en niños o mujeres en entornos de bajos ingresos; la generalización a adultos con hierro adecuado sigue siendo incierta a partir de estos ensayos. Los estudios de rendimiento del ejercicio son pequeños (n=10–21) y concentrados en atletas mujeres; si los beneficios se extienden a atletas hombres o en diferentes contextos de entrenamiento no es aparente en los datos recuperados. La seguridad a largo plazo (más allá de semanas a meses) y los resultados en poblaciones excluidas de la mayoría de ensayos — mujeres embarazadas sin deficiencia, personas con enfermedad renal, o aquellas en medicamentos que interactúan — no están representados en la muestra proporcionada.

appraisal_es.headline: El hierro para la anemia es respaldado de manera robusta por metanálisis grandes y consistentes; las afirmaciones sobre cognición, ejercicio y estado de ánimo se basan en muchos menos ensayos primarios (2–6 cada uno) con tamaños de muestra pequeños, lo que hace que esas calificaciones sean vulnerables a sesgo de reporte selectivo y sesgo de publicación.

concerns.issue: Cognición, ejercicio, estado de ánimo: evidencia primaria mínima
concerns.detail: Cognición (11 estudios) y ejercicio (5 estudios) y estado de ánimo (4 estudios) tienen cada uno una calificación Moderada a pesar de que el motor señala que caen 'por debajo del umbral para el nivel superior.' Para cognición, solo hay 6 RCTs disponibles; para ejercicio y estado de ánimo, solo 2–3 RCTs cada uno. En contraste, anemia tiene 71 RCTs. Con tan pocos ensayos primarios, un único estudio no publicado nulo o negativo podría cambiar sustancialmente la estimación agrupada; el efecto agrupado actual para cognición (SMD 0.46) también es modesto en términos absolutos y sensible a efectos de estudios pequeños.

concerns.issue: Brechas graves en el reporte del tamaño de muestra en resultados más pequeños
concerns.detail: Para cognición, solo 4 de 11 estudios reportan tamaño de muestra (mediana 1408); para ejercicio, solo 4 de 5 (mediana 23); para estado de ánimo, solo 2 de 4 (mediana 1408). Cuando los resúmenes omiten n, la precisión verdadera y la heterogeneidad no pueden ser evaluadas. La mediana de resultado de ejercicio de 23 es particularmente preocupante—tres de cinco estudios podrían ser muy pequeños, sin embargo no se puede extraer un efecto agrupado, lo que sugiere inconsistencia que no es completamente visible.

concerns.issue: Resultados de ejercicio y estado de ánimo: sin efecto agrupado reportado
concerns.detail: Para ejercicio y estado de ánimo, el motor señala 'efecto agrupado: ninguno extraíble,' indicando que los metanálisis no arrojaron una estimación combinada. Esto sugiere alta heterogeneidad, direcciones de efecto conflictivas, o datos escasos. Calificar estos como Moderados a pesar de la falta de una estimación agrupada sintetizada es inconsistente con las jerarquías de evidencia estándar y oscurece el estado actual del consenso.

concerns.issue: Resultado de anemia combina múltiples formulaciones de hierro y poblaciones
concerns.detail: Los 71 RCTs para anemia abarcan bisglicina ferrosa oral, hierro parenteral, y poblaciones que van desde donantes de sangre a mujeres embarazadas a niños. Aunque los metanálisis intentan estratificar por formulación y población, un único efecto agrupado (mean_diff 2.01) oscurece si la eficacia es uniforme o impulsada por subgrupos específicos (p. ej., mujeres embarazadas, anemia severa). El ensayo de 2026 sobre aplazamientos de donantes de sangre se menciona primero pero su hallazgo específico relativo a la estimación agrupada no se indica.

concerns.issue: Evidencia de cognición y estado de ánimo limitada a edad escolar y entornos de bajos recursos
concerns.detail: Los ensayos de cognición y estado de ánimo están fuertemente ponderados hacia niños en edad escolar y países de ingresos bajos y medios (visible en títulos: 'school-age children,' 'in Bangladeshi children,' 'in Ethiopia'). La generalizabilidad a poblaciones adultas, de altos ingresos, o sin anemia es incierta. El ensayo prenatal de 2024 sobre 'problemas conductuales' y el ensayo de fatiga de 2003 en mujeres sin anemia son excepciones, pero en conjunto comprenden solo 2 de 4 estudios de estado de ánimo.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: El papel del hierro en el transporte de oxígeno y síntesis de hemo respalda directamente la corrección de anemia y hemoglobina—un encaje mecanístico con la evidencia fuerte. Sin embargo, el salto del reemplazo de hierro a cognición y estado de ánimo es inferencialmente más largo: el hierro es un cofactor para el citocromo c oxidasa y síntesis de mielina, pero la base de evidencia no aclara si los beneficios cognitivos y del estado de ánimo son secundarios a la corrección de anemia (confusión) o efectos directos del reemplazo de hierro en individuos sin anemia. La revisión sistemática de 2025 sobre cognición en 'niños sin anemia' aborda esto, pero sus hallazgos específicos no se detallan en los registros, dejando el mecanismo incierto para estos resultados.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico señalaría que las calificaciones de cognición y estado de ánimo descansan en un puñado de ensayos pequeños (2–6 RCTs por resultado) con reporte incompleto, la mayoría realizados en niños en entornos de bajos recursos donde la desnutrición y parasitismo son confusores. El efecto agrupado para cognición (SMD 0.46) es modesto y no significativamente diferente de un efecto trivial una vez que se considera el sesgo de publicación. Los resultados de ejercicio y estado de ánimo carecen incluso de una estimación agrupada, sugiriendo que las síntesis encontraron evidencia insuficiente o conflictiva—clasificarlos como Moderados en lugar de Bajos es generoso. Para anemia, la calificación es segura, pero para los otros tres resultados, un metanálisis preregistrado con gráfico de embudo y prueba de Egger probablemente los degradaría.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Para cognición, ejercicio y estado de ánimo: una serie de RCTs adecuadamente potenciados (n > 200 por brazo), preregistrados en poblaciones sin anemia con medidas cognitivas/de estado de ánimo/de rendimiento estandarizadas y seguimiento a largo plazo (≥12 meses) aclararían si los efectos persisten y son clínicamente significativos. Para anemia: análisis de sensibilidad aislando eficacia por formulación (oral vs. parenteral), dosis y duración, y por estado de hierro basal (deficiente vs. normal) aclararían si la estimación agrupada se aplica ampliamente o es impulsada por subgrupos específicos.
